extracted.intended_audience: students and readers studying humor (undergraduate/introductory-level), instructors and scholars in humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for reading, writing about, and analyzing humor across cultural, cognitive, social, rhetorical, and ethical axes. Intended as an introductory framework for classroom study and critical inquiry into what makes things funny and what humor does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's significance: identity, culture, knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Humor is a relevant topic of study because of its significant role in the following three areas: identity (ontology), culture, and knowledge or meaning-making (epistemology).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how what we find funny reflects and shapes identity, reveals cultural values, and constructs or mediates knowledge. Examples: different cultural/geographic audiences (e.g., a twenty-something Chinese American in San Jose vs a twenty-something in Bangalore) may not find the same things funny. Consider both larger cultural influences and immediate social environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural context and exportability
rubrics_metrics.description: From Cultural Savvy: “Each culture has its own style of humor.” “Humor is very difficult to export.” “Humor requires an in-depth understanding of culture.” “Avoid ethnic-type humor, the following: stereotyping, sexist, off-color, cultural, or religious humor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating humor, account for cultural specificity and the risks of exporting jokes across cultures. Treat cross-cultural humor cautiously; investigate whether humor depends on local knowledge or insider status. Anti-pattern: assuming a joke will translate unchanged across cultures or ignoring cultural taboos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and meme dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet has become the medium par excellence for creating and disseminating humor; memes often function as an “inside joke” and when a meme “goes viral,” the circle of insiders enlarges, expanding what people consider funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how medium (memes, GIFs, YouTube) shapes humor (visual particularization, virality, inside-jokes). Examples: Epic Rap Battles (rely on cultural knowledge but also physical humor), viral 'Epic Fails' and pranking videos. Consider how the Internet globalizes local humor while still relying on cultural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between laughter and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Marshall Brain: “Laughter is the physiological response to humor.” Restak: we can laugh even in the absence of humor (e.g., frightened, embarrassed) and animals may laugh/react without making multiple interpretations of a situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, separate physiological/corporeal responses (laughter) from conceptual appreciation (humor). Do not equate laughter automatically with comprehension of humor; consider context and causes of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor requires conceptual understanding and cognitive processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor “involves a degree of creativity and the capacity for conceptual understanding and conceptual shifts.” Finding something funny often depends on making sense of an inconsistency between a script and a humorous situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the audience must perform conceptual shifts, draw on scripts/expectations, or resolve incongruities. Note neurological claims about networks in the cerebral cortex related to speech, general information, and appreciation of contradiction/illogicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The incongruity theory posits humor as an intellectual response to something that surprises us—to something that differs from the norm or accepted pattern. Our ability to 'resolve' the incongruity is crucial to appreciating the humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this framework to evaluate jokes that create unexpected contrasts, logical mismatches, or violated expectations. Scoring note: consider whether the incongruity is recognizable and resolvable by the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The superiority theory holds that we laugh because we feel superior to other people; laughter becomes an expression of this feeling and can be used to ridicule, bully, exclude, or to strengthen group solidarity or act as a social corrective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing humor, consider power dynamics and whether the joke creates or reinforces social hierarchies. Identify functions such as ridicule, exclusion, bonding, or social correction; watch for ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The relief theory ties humor and laughter to a biological function: humor and laughter release tension or excessive energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this lens to humor that functions to release anxiety, diffuse tension, or relieve social stress. Evaluate context to decide whether relief is the primary function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and cohesive functions of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter are social; laughter is contagious, possesses a 'cohesive effect,' is 'a friendly social gesture,' and 'facilitates social interaction.' Humor frequently occurs in social situations and play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how humor creates social bonds, signals group membership, or facilitates interaction. Recognize that the playful aspect can also be deployed seriously to challenge norms or enact protest. Examples: catching laughter, virtual shared experiences via media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical/persuasive power of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Used skillfully and purposefully, humor is an effective persuasive strategy or rhetorical tool; Cicero and Quintilian note that jocose manner and wit give pleasure, often advantage the speaker, dissipate hatred and anger, and can enhance ethos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humor in rhetorical texts or performances for strategic aims: does it strengthen speaker credibility, disarm opponents, relieve tension, or sway audience attitudes? Consider rarity and skill required for effective use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire as corrective/critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire, often humorous, critiques human vice and folly to improve human institutions or humanity and relies on devices such as parody and exaggeration; satirists use humor to expose and dismantle flaws rather than to destroy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging satirical humor, focus on intent (critique vs mere ridicule), technique (parody, exaggeration), and whether the satire illuminates institutional or social problems. Examples: SNL, The Daily Show, The Simpsons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic-racial humor: reinforcement vs subversion of stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethnic and racial humor often targets marginalized groups and 'very often, the dominant group remains unseen or simply implied.' Humorists may rework or subvert familiar stereotypes, but it can also reinforce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine whether humor challenges or perpetuates stereotypes. Consider historical context (minstrel shows, ethnic caricatures) and contemporary comedians who either subvert or reproduce stereotypes (e.g., Richard Pryor, Dave Chappelle, Margaret Cho). Ask: how does this humor shape perceptions of marginalized groups?

rubrics_metrics.name: Bawdy, off-color, and taboo humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Bawdy or scatological humor challenges taboos and has a long literary tradition (Aristophanes, Chaucer, Shakespeare). Contemporary crude/off-color humor can provoke debates about taste, acceptability, and free speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating bawdy humor, consider historical lineage, intent (challenge vs mere shock), and the boundaries of taste and acceptability. Note controversies and legal/ethical considerations (e.g., obscenity, free speech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's reliance on stereotypes and prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Using and getting humor very often rely on stereotypes and on our prior knowledge; humor often influences our perspectives on people different from us and on political and social issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the epistemic effects of humor: what prior assumptions does it presume or reinforce? Anti-pattern: uncritically relying on stereotypes, which can perpetuate racism, sexism, and classism. Consider how humor constructs knowledge about the world and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical inquiry prompts for studying humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested questions: When and why is something funny or not? Who decides what is funny? Can humor transcend cultures? How do race, class, and gender affect our sense of humor? Does humor promote inclusion or exclusion? What can we learn about ourselves and others by examining humor? Is humor ever innocent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as an evaluative checklist when reading, writing about, or producing humor. They guide ethical, cultural, political, and epistemological analysis and encourage reflexivity about the effects and responsibilities entailed in humor.
